questions.q: Which of these quantities is **continuous** rather than discrete?
options: Number of defects on a metre of cable
Number of leads converted out of 20
Number of calls in a minute
Minutes until the next customer arrives
questions.why: A waiting time can take any value in a range (2.37 minutes), so it is continuous and probabilities are areas under a curve. The other three are counts (0, 1, 2 …), which are discrete and have a probability for each exact value.

questions.q: A fuel station wants to model the **time between** randomly arriving cars. Which distribution fits the story best?
options: Exponential
Binomial
Uniform
Poisson
questions.why: The exponential describes waiting times between events of a Poisson process. Poisson is tempting because it is the same process, but it counts events per interval, not the gap between them. Binomial needs a fixed number of yes/no tries.

questions.q: Calls arrive as a Poisson process with λ = 3 per minute. Which statement about the number of calls per minute is true?
options: Mean 3, variance 3
Mean 3, variance 9
Mean 3, variance √3
Mean 3, variance unknown without more data
questions.why: For a Poisson distribution mean = variance = λ, so both are 3. Variance 9 confuses variance with λ²; √3 ≈ 1.73 is the SD, not the variance. This property is also the check for over-dispersion.

questions.q: A salesperson closes 10% of leads and has 20 leads this week. What is the probability she closes **exactly 2**?
questions.why: Binomial: (20 choose 2) × 0.1² × 0.9¹⁸ = 190 × 0.01 × 0.1501 = 0.285. 0.010 forgets both the 190 orderings and the failures; 0.100 is just 2/20; 0.190 is P(exactly 3).

questions.q: Daily complaint counts at a branch have mean 4 and variance 19. Someone proposes a Poisson model. What does the data suggest?
options: Poisson fits well, since counts are always Poisson
The data are over-dispersed (variance far above the mean); a negative binomial model is likely to fit better
The data are under-dispersed; use a binomial
Switch to a normal distribution because the variance is large
questions.why: A Poisson model forces variance = mean. A variance almost five times the mean is over-dispersion, often caused by bad days clustering, and a negative binomial allows for it. A normal model would still ignore that the data are small counts that cannot go below zero.

questions.q: Calls arrive at λ = 3 per minute (Poisson). What is the **smallest** per-minute capacity that keeps overloaded minutes (more calls than capacity) below 1%?
options: 4 calls
6 calls
7 calls
8 calls
questions.why: P(more than 6) = 0.0335, P(more than 7) = 0.0119 (still just over 1%), P(more than 8) = 0.0038. So 8 is the first capacity under 1%. Planning near the average of 3 or 4 guarantees frequent overloads.

questions.q: Gaps between cars at a fuel station are exponential with mean 2 minutes. No car has arrived for 5 minutes. What is the probability the attendant waits **more than 3 more minutes**?
options: 0.018, because the total wait would be 8 minutes
0.223, the same as for a fresh wait, because the exponential is memoryless
0.082, because 5 minutes have already passed
Lower than 0.1, because a car is now "due"
questions.why: The exponential is memoryless: P(wait > 3) = e^(−3/2) = 0.223 whatever has already happened. 0.018 = e^(−8/2) wrongly treats it as a fresh 8-minute wait. The idea that a car is "due" is the gambler's fallacy for random arrivals.

questions.q: In an interview: "A colleague models daily product returns, which average 0.8 per day, with a normal distribution. What is your critique?"
options: Fine, because the normal approximates everything
Use a uniform distribution instead, since every count is equally likely
The normal is wrong here: small counts are discrete, skewed and cannot be negative; use a Poisson (or negative binomial if over-dispersed)
Use a t-distribution because the sample is small
questions.why: With a mean below 1, most days are 0 or 1 and the normal would put real probability on negative returns. The normal approximation only works for large counts (for a binomial, when n·p and n·(1 − p) are both at least about 10). The t-distribution is for test statistics, not raw counts.
